The Night the Power Went Out

At six the refrigerator stopped its humming
and the whole apartment seemed to lean forward,
listening. My sister said a word
our mother pretended not to hear.

I had four problems left of twenty,
my pencil still warm in my hand,
and I was angry the way you are angry
at weather, which cannot be argued with.

We found the candles in the kitchen drawer
behind the batteries and the birthday string,
and my father, who is not a patient man,
took his time with the match.

Light came up the walls like water rising.
Our shadows grew enormous and polite.
Across the courtyard other windows
were filling, one by one, with the same small fires,

and I understood that everyone I had ever
resented for their television
was sitting, as we sat, around a saucer,
saying almost nothing, being kind.

My sister asked what people did before.
My mother said: this.
Out past the roofline, where the city keeps
its own bright weather, I could see

three stars I had not been told about,
ordinary as nails, and holding.
When the lights came back at nine
we cheered, and I was sorry.

choices: Helping a parent search a kitchen drawer
Watching a programme in a window across the courtyard
Working through the last of a homework assignment
Counting the stars above the roofline
Setting out candles for a birthday
correct_answer: Working through the last of a homework assignment
explanation: The second stanza places the speaker mid-assignment: 'I had four problems left of twenty, / my pencil still warm in my hand.' That is what the blackout interrupts.

distractor_rationales.Helping a parent search a kitchen drawer: The drawer is searched after the blackout, and by the family together, not by the speaker beforehand.
distractor_rationales.Watching a programme in a window across: The courtyard windows are noticed later, and what fills them is candlelight.

The company's new production of a familiar comedy opens with a gamble, and for about twenty minutes the gamble pays. The director has stripped the stage to a single long table and nine chairs: no painted parlour, no windows, and, most of all, no doors to slam. Since the play is built on slammed doors, this is not a small decision. In place of doors the actors use the chairs, stepping over them, turning them to face away, carrying them off into the wings when a character is supposed to have left the house. The effect at first is exhilarating. We are asked to build the rooms ourselves, and we do.

The trouble is that the device has one speed. A slammed door is loud, sudden and final; a chair carried off is none of those things. By the second act, when the plot demands four entrances and exits inside a minute, the stage becomes a furniture removal, and the audience laughs at the wrong thing - at the labour of the actors rather than at the lie the character is telling. The performers are not at fault. The actor playing the aunt gives the sharpest reading of that part I have seen anywhere, finding real grief under lines that are usually played for noise, and the young man in the servant's role has a gift for stillness that the production, to its credit, lets him use.

I want to be fair to the idea. A bare stage does force attention onto the language, and this text can bear that attention; there were passages last night that I heard properly for the first time. Nor is the choice merely a way of saving money, since the lighting alone must have cost what a set would. But an idea that clarifies one act and defeats the next is a half-idea, and a director's job includes knowing the hour at which to abandon his own best invention. Keep the table. Keep the aunt. Give the poor company its doors back, and this would be the production that the rest of the design deserves.

explanation: The review holds two things together: the gamble 'pays' for twenty minutes and the acting is excellent, but the device 'has one speed' and collapses under the second act's traffic. The closing advice - keep the table, restore the doors - is that judgment in practical form.

My uncle keeps the chart above the sink,
a page of numbers small as grains of rice,
and every morning, before the kettle,
he runs one finger down the column.

For a year I thought this was a habit
like touching the doorframe on the way out,
the sort of thing a man does because his father did,
and I did not ask.

Then a Tuesday in October he said, Come,
and we walked to the flats at a quarter past six
where the water had gone off somewhere else
and left the whole bay standing open -

long ribs of sand, a stranded orange buoy,
a boat sitting down in the mud like a cow,
the mussel beds black and shining
as a kept promise.

Two hours, he said. Then it comes back
across this ground, faster than a man walks.
I looked at the drying sand and did not believe him.
But I had seen the page: six forty-two,

and a number that meant how far,
and the small letter L beside it
that meant the sea would be low,
and then would not.

Now I check it too, before the kettle.
It is not that I am afraid of the water.
It is that someone wrote down, years ago,
exactly when the door would stand open,

and where I live, that is the nearest thing
to being told a secret
and being trusted with it.

Every spring the branch library at the end of my street posts its year's figures in the front window, and every spring the figure set in the largest type is circulation: the number of items checked out and carried home. I understand the appeal. It counts a real act, it can be set beside last year's, and it fits in a headline. I would still like the library to stop leading with it, because a library that manages itself toward that number will slowly become a worse library.

Consider what circulation cannot see. A student who spends four afternoons a week at a table because her own apartment is too loud to think in borrows nothing. A man who comes in out of the cold and works through the newspapers borrows nothing. The woman at the desk who spent twenty minutes last Thursday showing a retired machinist how to attach a document to an email produced no checkout at all, and that twenty minutes was, by any honest account, the most useful thing the building did that day.

The objection to my position is fair, and I should state it properly. A library must report something to the people who pay for it, and the alternatives are soft. Hours of seat use, questions answered at the desk, classes held - these are harder to count and far easier to inflate, and a director who leans on them can conceal a real decline for years. So I would not throw the circulation figure away. It measures one thing well, and a sudden collapse in it would be worth explaining.

But it should be one line in a paragraph, not the headline in the window. What a branch gives a neighbourhood is a warm room with a knowledgeable adult in it and no requirement to buy anything, and there is no other building on my street of which that is true. When the only number we publish is the number of books that leave, we invite the council to imagine that the books are the point, and then to ask, reasonably enough, why the room around them costs so much.

explanation: The first paragraph asks the library 'to stop leading with it'; the third refuses to 'throw the circulation figure away'; the last asks for 'one line in a paragraph, not the headline in the window.' The claim is about prominence, not about abolition.

Eighty photographs of shopfronts, made over eleven years in a single county, hang in four rooms, and for the length of the first room I was entirely persuaded. The photographer works in flat morning light and stands square to the glass, so that every picture has the same grammar: a door, a window, a hand-lettered sign, and, reflected faintly in the glass, the street behind her. Hung in a row, the pictures begin to argue. You notice that the lettering grows more professional and less legible; that the goods in the windows change from things that were made to things that were shipped; that by the fourth room almost nothing on any street is being repaired.

Then there are the labels. Beside each photograph the gallery has hung a paragraph telling you what to feel about it. One announces that a laundry's shuttered door is a monument to a vanished solidarity. Another explains that a rack of plastic buckets interrogates the logic of disposability. These sentences are not exactly wrong. They are arriving too early, and in the wrong voice. The photographs had already said the harder half of all this, quietly and without adjectives, and the effect of reading the label first - and everyone reads the label first - is that you go to the picture to confirm a verdict rather than to look at it.

I can imagine the gallery's defence, and it is not a frivolous one. A visitor given nothing at all may look for four seconds and move on, and a short text can slow that visitor down. But there is a difference between telling her where a photograph was taken, what the shop sold and in what year it closed - all of which this exhibition does well, and none of which the pictures can supply on their own - and telling her what the photograph means. Every few years somebody proposes to fix the long race. The suggestions vary - shorten it, break it into heats, show only the leaders - but the reasoning is always the same: nothing happens for most of an hour, and audiences will not sit still for it. The reasoning has a point buried in it, and I will come back to that point. It is wrong about what the event is.

A short race is a comparison of top speeds. You watch eight bodies do the same thing at once, the fastest wins, and it is thrilling, and it is over before you have chosen anybody to care about. A long race is a comparison of decisions. In the ninth lap a runner lying fourth works out that she has one surge and not two, and spends it, and you can see her decide. The runner who wins may have spent twenty minutes in fifth place doing arithmetic - how much is left, how much the leader has used, what the wind on the back straight will cost. None of that exists in a race that lasts ten seconds, and none of it can be manufactured by cutting to the leaders, because the leaders are precisely the part of the picture where the decisions have already been made.

Now the point I promised to come back to, which is a real one: the middle of a long race is genuinely hard to watch, and the sport has not helped itself. Commentary that names only the front three, and cameras that follow the same three, teach an audience that the rest is filler. A spectator who has never run has no way to know that the pace has quietly risen, or that a runner who drifts wide on a bend has lost more than a stride. That is a failure of coverage, not a failure of the event. Show the gap closing at the back. Put the lap times on screen where newcomers can read them.

Do that, and the hour stops being empty. Shorten the race instead, and you will have kept the audience by removing the reason to watch.
